claim_details.claim: Research and philosophical debate about innate knowledge is ongoing and deeply divided. On one side, empirical research holds that the human brain possesses important innate knowledge — such as the understanding that three-dimensional objects persist even when not observed — which was acquired through evolution this view is supported by psychological research showing that babies and dogs demonstrate innate object permanence ; researchers like Noam Chomsky have similarly argued that the capacity to acquire language must be something we are born with, though participants across studies tend to be biased against accepting that knowledge can be inborn, partly because innate knowledge challenges our intuitive expectations

On the other side, 17th-century philosopher John Locke argued that the mind is a tabula rasa (blank slate) at birth and that all knowledge is demonstrably acquired through sensory experience, rejecting the existence of innate knowledge entirely ; Locke's empiricist position is further reinforced by the observation that truths requiring reason to discover cannot be considered innate, as it would be contradictory to claim men know something innately yet remain ignorant of it until reason is applied

Philosophical traditions differ significantly on this question: while Plato and Descartes proposed that humans possess innate mathematical and conceptual knowledge , the emerging scientific consensus has been to treat innate knowledge as a contested hypothesis, with ongoing psychological research still working to settle the question
